text:
Avatar fingerprinting addresses the problem of determining whether a synthetic avatar video is driven by its legitimate user or not, focusing on identity cues preserved in facial motion dynamics rather than visual appearance alone. The problem is also related to behavioral biometrics [27, 28], where identity is inferred from human dynamic patterns such as gait, keystroke, or facial motion. Unlike traditional face recognition, which relies heavily on appearance cues, avatar fingerprinting must operate under conditions where appearance is synthetically generated and therefore unreliable.

This section provides a revision of the state of the art in avatar fingerprinting. Sec. 2.1 summarizes recent advances in photorealistic talking-head avatar generation. Sec. 2.2 describes publicly available databases for avatar fingerprinting. Sec. 2.3 reviews avatar fingerprinting approaches.

document_title: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
Photorealistic talking-head avatar generation aims to animate a target identity using the facial motion and head pose extracted from a driving signal, typically a video sequence. This task is also commonly referred to as portrait animation [29], motion transfer [30], or talking-head reenactment [31]. It is important to remark that this task differs from related problems such as novel-view synthesis [32], full 3D head reconstruction [33], or audio-driven animation [34], as the goal is to preserve the appearance of a reference identity while faithfully transferring motion dynamics from another source.

Early approaches to facial reenactment relied on parametric face models and 3D morphable models to retarget expressions and head pose, enabling real-time portrait manipulation and reenactment [35, 36]. The emergence of deep generative models enabled realistic reenactment from minimal input, particularly through motion transfer methods that animate a single portrait using learned keypoint dynamics [13, 37]. Subsequent advances in neural rendering and implicit scene representations improved realism and view consistency [38, 39], while recent diffusion-based video generation techniques have further increased photorealism and temporal coherence [24, 40].

These methods can be broadly categorized according to their underlying representation and synthesis strategy as follow:

document_title: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
These methods can be broadly categorized according to their underlying representation and synthesis strategy as follow:

- Neural rendering approaches, such as NeRF-based (Neural Radiance Field) models, represent the head as a continuous radiance field learned from images [38, 41]. While they achieve high visual fidelity and view consistency, they typically require multi-view data and are computationally expensive, which limits their applicability in real-time or one-shot scenarios.
- Gaussian splatting methods provide a more efficient alternative by representing the head as a set of 3D Gaussian primitives [16, 42, 43]. These approaches enable real-time rendering and controllable animation through parametric face models, although they may exhibit minor geometric inconsistencies.
- Image-based warping methods operate directly in the image domain by transferring motion using learned keypoints or flow fields [37, 44]. These methods are computationally efficient and well-suited for

real-time applications. Recent works such as LivePortrait [23] demonstrate that large-scale training and improved architectures can yield high-quality and stable animations despite the lack of 3D modeling.

- Diffusion-based methods represent the current state of the art in visual quality. By conditioning video diffusion models on identity and motion signals, they generate temporally coherent and highly realistic avatar videos [24]. These approaches offer strong generalization capabilities but typically incur higher computational costs.

Across these paradigms, different design choices lead to variations in motion transfer fidelity, temporal consistency, and artifact characteristics. These differences are particularly relevant for avatar fingerprinting, as they can influence how identity-related facial dynamics are preserved or distorted. Consequently, evaluating avatar fingerprinting systems across multiple avatar generation methods is essential to assess their robustness under realistic synthesis variability, which is the purpose of the present article.

document_title: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
To date, the number of public databases and benchmarks specifically designed for avatar fingerprinting is very limited. The NVFAIR database introduced by NVIDIA [7] is currently the largest collection of reenacted talkinghead videos, with more than 600,000 videos. NVFAIR comprises scripted and free-form monologues from 46 captured subjects (real data) as well as synthetic reenactments generated with three methods (FaceVid2Vid [13], TPS [14], and LIA [15]), although they are considered old-fashioned nowadays in comparison to state-of-the-art avatar generators, as discussed in Sec. 2.1. In total NVFAIR covers 161 unique identities (by including additional CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21] speakers) with self- and crossreenactments. Access to NVFAIR is restricted via a request form. Also, benchmarking is not possible as the proposed avatar fingerprinting system is not publicly available.

To the best of our knowledge, the only fully public avatar fingerprinting database and benchmark so far is the GAGAvatar-Benchmark [12]. However, it only covers a single talking-head avatar generator (GAGAvatar [22]), limiting diversity in appearance and motion dynamics.

The proposed AVAPrintDB and benchmark is publicly available and covers multiple up-to-date photorealistic avatar generators (GAGAvatar [22], LivePortrait [23] and HunyuanPortrait [24]) and varied source domains (e.g., generator and dataset shift), allowing to evaluate state-of-the-art avatar fingerprinting systems in realistic scenarios.

Finally, as already mentioned in Sec. 1, it is important to highlight that the task of avatar fingerprinting differs from the task of DeepFakes detection [8, 9, 10], where the main goal is to distinguish real from synthetic content. As a result, public databases in the topic of DeepFakes detection cannot be used for avatar fingerprinting.

document_title: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
The task of avatar fingerprinting is formulated as a pairwise decision problem: given two avatar videos, the goal is to determine whether they are driven by the same underlying identity or not. This differs from authentication, which evaluates a sample against a claimed identity (e.g., access control scenarios), and from identification, where a sample is matched against a gallery of known identities. Avatar fingerprinting constitutes the most fundamental setting, as it isolates the ability of a model to capture identity-dependent behavioral signals without relying on predefined identity classes.

Early works on avatar fingerprinting demonstrated that such behavioral cues persist through avatar generation. In [7], identity was modeled through facial landmark dynamics using temporal convolutional networks, showing that user-specific motion patterns can be discriminative even in highly realistic avatars (they achieved around 87% AUC in their best setting). Similarly, [11, 12] proposed a graph-based approach that captures structured relationships between facial landmarks over time, obtaining similar results in their respective experiments (86.6% and 83% AUC respectively).

A common characteristic of existing approaches is their reliance on landmarkbased representations, which provide invariance to appearance and mitigate the influence of rendering artifacts. However, this design choice may also limit the ability to capture fine-grained visual cues present in the pixel domain, particularly those related to texture-dependent motion or subtle temporal inconsistencies. For this reason, in the present work, we explore for the first time the use of Foundation Models (DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26]) for avatar fingerprinting, which can encode richer spatio-temporal information without explicit geometric modeling.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
We select two widely used video datasets in the literature as they consider realistic scenarios for avatar fingerprinting: CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21]. Our selection is guided by three main considerations. First, both datasets are distributed under permissive licenses that allow redistribution and derivative use, making them suitable for constructing and releasing a reproducible benchmark. Second, they have been employed in prior work on avatar fingerprinting and behavioral biometric analysis, including [7, 12, 45], which facilitates continuity. Third, they include structured variations in emotional expression and scripted utterances. These characteristics enable controlled experimental protocols in which different subjects can be evaluated while producing identical sentences and emotional expressions. Such control is essential for avatar fingerprinting studies, as it allows identity-related motion cues to be isolated from linguistic content, affective expression, and other confounding factors. For example, the datasets make it possible to compare avatars of different individuals speaking the same sentence with similar affect, or the same individual rendered through different avatar pipelines, enabling fine-grained evaluation of biometric consistency.

Initially, we also considered the real videos from the NVFAIR dataset [7], which includes additional videoconferencing recordings from 46 participants. Unfortunately, its licensing terms restrict redistribution and limit demographic analysis (e.g., ethnicity, age, and gender), so we could not included in the proposed benchmark. Consequently, CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21] provide the best balance between legal permissibility, experimental control, and comparability with prior avatar fingerprinting research.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
CREMA-D [20] (Crowd-sourced Emotional Multimodal Actors Dataset) is a large-scale audiovisual corpus designed to study emotional speech and multimodal expression. It contains 7,438 video recordings of 91 actors (48 male, 43 female) between 20 and 74 years, representing a demographically diverse group with respect to race and ethnicity. Actors were recorded under controlled indoor conditions with frontal viewpoints, consistent lighting and high-quality audio capture.

Each participant delivers 12 semantically neutral sentences, which are performed using multiple emotional expressions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, neutral, and sadness. The recordings exhibit natural variation in intensity and articulation while preserving consistent linguistic content. All videos were recorded on 460 × 360 pixels at 30 FPS.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
RAVDESS [21] (Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech and Song) is a high-quality audiovisual corpus designed for research on emotional expression and multimodal speech. It includes recordings from 24 professional actors (12 female, 12 male) speaking and singing with a range of emotional expressions. In this article, we use the speech subset, which contains 1,440 video recordings corresponding to two repetitions of 60 scripted utterances produced by each actor.

Recordings were captured under tightly controlled studio conditions, including uniform lighting, frontal framing, neutral backgrounds, and highfidelity audio and video. Actors deliver semantically neutral sentences using multiple emotional states (neutral, calm, happy, sad, angry, fearful, surprised, and disgust) with two intensity levels for all emotions but neutral. All videos are 1280 × 720 pixels and were recorded at 30FPS.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text: A key aspect of our proposed AVAPrintDB is the inclusion of multiple state-of-the-art avatar generators, each relying on different modeling assumptions and motion transfer mechanisms: one from the Gaussian splatting family (GAGAvatar [22]), one from the warping-based family (LivePortrait [23]), and one from the diffusion-based family (HunyuanPortrait [24]). These three generators are selected as they represent distinct synthesis paradigms and therefore introduce different types of motion transfer artifacts that may influence the avatar fingerprinting task. They are specifically selected due to practical considerations of availability, efficiency, and quality. GAGAvatar [22] is a one-shot 3D Gaussian head avatar method that reconstructs a controllable 3D head from a single image in a single forward pass. It is lightweight in GPU memory and offers real-time reenactment speeds thanks to its efficient 3D Gaussian representation, making it easy to use for our purposes. LivePortrait [23] provides a fast, efficient 2D animation solution with minimal memory overhead, and the code/models are publicly available. LivePortrait's ease of use and high speed, combined with qualitatively good visual results, made it a practical choice for our comparisons. Finally, HunyuanPortrait [24] considers a state-of-the-art diffusion model. Although diffusion models are heavier, HunyuanPortrait is open-source and produces great visual fidelity and temporal consistency. Its inclusion allows to evaluate a high-quality diffusion approach against the faster lightweight methods.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text: From a biometric behavioral perspective, the generation process can be interpreted as a transformation that maps real facial motion into a synthetic domain. Ideally, this transformation should preserve identity-specific temporal patterns while altering appearance. However, in practice, avatar generators may introduce biases, artifacts, or normalization effects that partially suppress or modify these cues. As a result, models trained or evaluated on a single generator may inadvertently learn generator-specific artifacts instead of robust behavioral patterns. To address this limitation, our proposed benchmark incorporates multiple generators with diverse characteristics, enabling systematic evaluation under intra- and cross-generator conditions. This design allows us to analyze whether avatar fingerprinting systems generalize across synthesis pipelines or rely on artifacts tied to a specific generator.

Each generated video is defined by a target identity (which determines the avatar appearance) and a driving identity (which provides the motion dynamics). This setup enables both self-reenactment (same target and driver) and cross-reenactment (different target and driver), as shown in Fig. 1, which are essential for evaluating avatar fingerprinting. Additionally, all avatar videos are generated using a consistent protocol. For the target images, we manually select a single frontal, neutralexpression frame per subject from the curated dataset. Therefore, each driver identity contributes exactly 8 ×N cross-reenactment instances (eight targets, N driving videos), and each of these instances is rendered with all three generators, yielding 8 ×N × 3 synthetic videos per driver identity in the cross-reenactment setting.

The resulting AVAPrintDB provides: (i) self-reenactments for genuine verification (same target and driver), (ii) cross-reenactments for impersonation (different target and driver), and (iii) generator-aligned triplicates for every target-driver-video tuple. This structure supports a wide range of protocols, including intra-generator and cross-generator testing, cross-dataset generalization, and combined training on multiple generators with evaluation on held-out generators, as we describe next in Sec. 4.

As a result, the proposed AVAPrintDB comprises a total of 66,069 avatar videos, generated from 109 identities across three avatar generators and two source datasets. The distribution of videos across source datasets and reenactment types is summarized in Table 2.

text: Beyond the proposed AVAPrintDB itself, we also define a standardized experimental benchmark, including publicly available avatar fingerprinting systems, identity-disjoint development and evaluation splits, predefined verification trial lists, and evaluation procedures. This design ensures that different avatar fingerprinting systems can be compared under identical conditions, facilitating reproducible research and fair benchmarking. This section is organized as follows: the details of the proposed experimental protocol are included in Sec. 4.1 whereas in Sec. 4.2 we describe the avatar fingerprinting systems considered in the benchmark, including the exploration for the first time of Foundation Models (DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26]).

text:
Using the above protocol, we define three main experimental scenarios:

- Intra-dataset, intra-generator: the development and evaluation of the avatar fingerprinting systems are performed on avatar videos generated from the same source dataset and with the same avatar generator. These are the baseline results.
- Intra-dataset, cross-generator: the development and evaluation of the avatar fingerprinting systems are performed on the same source dataset, but the avatar generator used for development differs from the one used at the final evaluation. This evaluates robustness to avatar synthesismodel shift while keeping the underlying source domain fixed.
- Cross-dataset, intra-generator: the development and evaluation of the avatar fingerprinting systems are performed using the same avatar generator, but the source dataset differs between development and the final evaluation. This setting measures generalization across acquisition conditions, subject populations, and dataset-specific biases.

All these experimental scenarios allow us to disentangle three important axes of variation in avatar fingerprinting: identity generalization (unseen subjects), generator generalization (unseen avatar synthesis pipelines), and dataset generalization (unseen source domains). This benchmark provides a controlled framework for understanding whether avatar fingerprinting systems learn robust identity-related motion cues or overfit to datasetor generator-specific artifacts.

text: Similar to previous approaches in the literature [7, 11, 12], we assess avatar fingerprinting performance using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC). This metric measures the ability of the system to separate target from non-target trials across all possible decision thresholds, and is particularly appropriate here because it is thresholdindependent and robust to moderate class imbalance in the number of genuine and impostor pairs. Unless otherwise stated, all results in the article are reported in terms of AUC (%).

To advance in the topic of avatar fingerprinting under realistic synthesis conditions, we require systems that are reproducible, fully specified, and publicly accessible. Although recent studies have been presented in the literature [7, 11], none of them have released their implementations, training pipelines, or pretrained weights, making it impossible to reproduce their results or conduct fair comparative evaluations.

For this reason, in the proposed benchmark we evaluate our publicly available graph-based avatar fingerprinting system 8 presented in [12], which, to the best of our knowledge, is currently the only fully reproducible implementation. This system, as depicted in Fig. 2, takes as input a set of 109 facial landmarks per frame in an avatar video, structured as graphs. Then a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) generates a graph embedding for each graph (frame), and finally the aggregation mechanism (temporal attention pooling) yields a single embedding for the video. By evaluating the only publicly available avatar fingerprinting system on a more diverse dataset, we aim to provide insights into the robustness and limitations of current technology and to establish a foundation for future comparative studies once additional methods become publicly accessible.

In addition, we explore for the first time the use of public Foundational Models and attention-based neural networks for avatar fingerprinting. Foundation Models provide a complementary perspective, analyzing whether general-purpose visual representations can capture behavioral biometric cues in avatar videos. Concretely, we use DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26] as framelevel feature extractors. Fig. 3 provides a graphical representation of the proposed avatar fingerprinting system. text:
We first analyze the performance of avatar fingerprinting systems under the most controlled experimental setting: intra-dataset and intra-generator scenario. In this configuration, development and evaluation of the avatar fingerprinting systems are performed using avatar videos generated from the same source dataset and with the same avatar generator. This setting allows to assess the intrinsic ability of the evaluated systems to capture identityrelated motion dynamics from synthetic avatar videos. Table 5 reports the performance in terms of AUC (%). Results are presented for each combination of development/evaluation dataset (CREMA-D and RAVDESS) and avatar generator (GAGAvatar, LivePortrait, and HunyuanPortrait). We also include the performance of the "Fusion" approach, where the verification scores obtained for each pair (one per model) are averaged at the score level.

First, we analyze the performance on each individual dataset. In general we can observe higher AUC values on the CREMA-D dataset than on RAVDESS across all models and generators (e.g., 93.8% vs 83.0% on GAGAvatar for the Fusion approach). This difference can be attributed to the larger number of identities and videos available in CREMA-D, which provides more variability during training and therefore facilitates the learning of identitydiscriminative motion patterns.

text:
First, we analyze the performance on each individual dataset. In general we can observe higher AUC values on the CREMA-D dataset than on RAVDESS across all models and generators (e.g., 93.8% vs 83.0% on GAGAvatar for the Fusion approach). This difference can be attributed to the larger number of identities and videos available in CREMA-D, which provides more variability during training and therefore facilitates the learning of identitydiscriminative motion patterns.

The choice of avatar generator also has a noticeable impact on the performance of the avatar fingerprinting task. Across most configurations, avatars generated with LivePortrait tend to yield slightly higher AUC values than those generated with GAGAvatar or HunyuanPortrait (e.g., for the CREMAD scenario, the Fusion approach achieves 95.2% AUC for LivePortrait whereas this performance is reduced to 93.8% and 87.6% for the GAGAvatar and HunyuanPortrait, respectively). This may reflect differences in the motion transfer characteristics and visual artifacts produced by the generators, which can affect how identity-related motion cues are preserved in the resulting videos. In particular, LivePortrait may produce more stable and temporally consistent motion patterns, which facilitates the extraction of discriminative behavioral features, whereas other generators may introduce smoothing effects or artifacts that partially distort such cues.

Nevertheless, avatar fingerprinting systems based on the use of Foundation Models (DINOv2 and CLIP) achieve competitive performance too (e.g., GAGAvatar=87.0%, LivePortrait=88.8%, and HunyuanPortrait=79.8% for the DINOv2 approach). This means that high-level visual representations extracted from large-scale pretrained models can also capture discriminative motion patterns relevant for avatar fingerprinting. For RAVDESS dataset the behavior of the three different systems is similar to the CREMA-D dataset experiment.

For each source dataset independently (CREMA-D and RAVDESS), we train the avatar fingerprinting systems on avatars generated by one generator and evaluate them on avatars generated by a different generator. When training on GAGAvatar, the Graph system shows relatively good cross-generator generalization on CREMA-D, with moderate drops of 1.5 and -2.9 AUC points when evaluated on LivePortrait and HunyuanPortrait, respectively. In contrast, the DINOv2 (-20.3) and CLIP (-14.6) systems are significantly more affected, with drops of up to -20.3 (DINOv2) and -14.6 (CLIP). Training on LivePortrait leads to substantially worse generalization. Similar behavior is observed on RAVDESS (e.g., -10.0 for Fusion when transferring to GAGAvatar). Training on LivePortrait leads to substantially worse generalization. On CREMA-D, drops reach -8.5 (GAGAvatar) and -11.4 (HunyuanPortrait) for the Graph system, and up to -18.9 (from 88.8% to 69.9%) for DINOv2. Similar behavior is observed on RAVDESS (e.g., -10.0 for Fusion when transferring to GAGAvatar). This suggests that models trained on LivePortrait overfit to generator-specific characteristics, particularly on CREMA-D.

When training on HunyuanPortrait, results are more mixed. In some cases, the Graph system even improves when evaluated on other generators (e.g., +3.9 on CREMA-D, going from 83.5% AUC to 87.4% AUC). However, this effect is not consistent, and Foundation Models such as DINOv2 (up to -16.3%) still show notable drops, indicating that generalization depends on both the generator and the representation. We hypothesize that some generators may preserve behavioral cues in a way that transfers better across synthesis pipelines, whereas others may induce representations that are more generator-specific. One possible explanation is that the more constrained or artifact-prone generators encourage the avatar fingerprinting systems to focus on coarse but stable motion patterns that remain observable under other synthesis conditions. On the other hand, generators producing visually cleaner or more stylized outputs may lead the verifier to partially rely on synthesis-specific regularities that do not transfer well.

Unlike the cross-generator setting described in Sec. 5.2, the results in Table 7 do not show a uniform degradation under domain shift. Instead, they reveal a marked asymmetry depending on transfer direction. When training on CREMA-D and testing on RAVDESS, all methods suffer substantial performance drops. However, when training on RAVDESS and testing on CREMA-D, models often maintain performance or even improve over the intra-dataset reference. This indicates that current avatar fingerprinting systems are influenced by dataset-specific biases, but also that some datasets may promote representations that transfer better than others. This means that the learned representation is influenced not only by identity-dependent motion cues, but also by domain-specific characteristics from the source data.

Focusing first on the CREMA-D → RAVDESS transfer (i.e., training on CREMA-D and evaluating on RAVDESS), all models exhibit a significant drop in performance. For example, the Graph system decreases by -10.9,

This asymmetric behavior can be explained by differences in dataset characteristics. CREMA-D contains a larger number of identities and samples, providing greater variability in facial motion, expression, and subject appearance. While this diversity is beneficial for learning rich representations, it may also lead to systems capturing dataset-specific patterns that do not generalize well. On the other hand, RAVDESS is smaller and more controlled, with more consistent recording conditions and more exaggerated, actor-driven expressions. Training on such data may encourage the systems to focus on more stable and salient motion cues, which transfer more effectively to the more diverse CREMA-D dataset.

text:
This section provides a preliminary fairness analysis of the selected avatar fingerprinting systems using the soft-biometric annotations available in our proposed AVAPrintDB (i.e., gender, ethnicity, and age). For more details, we refer to Table 3. Results are reported in Table 8 and 9 in terms of AUC (%) for each subgroup, source dataset and avatar generator. We consider the intra-dataset and intra-generator scenario.

The fairness analysis is conducted at the level of verification trials. Each trial consists of an enrollment video V e and a test video V t , where the enrollment sample always corresponds to a self-reenactment (genuine avatar), while the test sample may be either genuine or impostor. To assess demographic effects in a consistent manner, we define all subgroup labels (gender, ethnicity, and age) based exclusively on the enrollment identity, i.e., the identity associated with V e . This design choice reflects the intended application scenario of avatar-based authentication, where the system verifies whether a query sample matches a claimed identity. In particular, the enrollment identity represents the individual who may be subject to impersonation, and therefore constitutes the reference point for analyzing fairness.

Analyzing the results of CREMA-D in Table 8, performance across gender groups is generally balanced, although some differences appear depending on the avatar fingerprinting system and avatar generator. All systems show small gaps for GAGAvatar, but larger discrepancies arise for LivePortrait and HunyuanPortrait. For instance, DINOv2 performs better for male subjects in LivePortrait (93.6% vs 84.4%), and CLIP also shows a consistent advantage for male subjects. On RAVDESS (Table 9), trends are less consistent: the Graph system favors female subjects (e.g., 82.1% vs 70.8% for LivePortrait), while DINOv2 and CLIP show mixed behavior. Overall, gender effects are not systematic, suggesting that they depend on the interaction between dataset, generator, and feature representation.

section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
Ethnicity-related variability is more pronounced. On CREMA-D (Table 8), all systems tend to perform best on the Caucasian group, which is also the most represented (e.g., 90.5% AUC for the Graph system on GAGAvatar). Asian and Hispanic groups generally achieve lower performance, particularly for HunyuanPortrait, although this pattern is not uniform across systems. For example, CLIP achieves its best performance for the Hispanic group in GAGAvatar (92.7%). The African American group shows competitive results across systems. On RAVDESS (Table 9), analysis is limited due to lower diversity, but variability across groups is still observed. These results suggest that ethnicity-related differences are influenced by both dataset imbalance and system representation.

Age-related differences do not follow a consistent trend. While younger groups (20-45) often achieve strong performance, the older group (46-60) does not systematically degrade. On CREMA-D (Table 8), in some cases performance drops (e.g., 69.6% for the Graph system on GAGAvatar), whereas in others it remains competitive or even improves (e.g., 94.5% for DINOv2 on LivePortrait). Similar variability is observed in RAVDESS (Table 9). This indicates that age effects depend on the combination of dataset, generator, and system, rather than following a uniform pattern. The limited number of older subjects further restricts strong conclusions.

These findings highlight the importance of balanced datasets and suggest that both system designs and avatar generation pipelines can influence how identity-related motion cues are preserved across populations.

document_title: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
section_path: Leveraging Avatar Fingerprinting: A Multi-Generator Photorealistic Talking-Head Public Database and Benchmark
text:
This article introduces AVAPrintDB, a publicly available multi-generator photorealistic talking-head avatar database and benchmark for the task of avatar fingerprinting. Its main strength is that it enables, for the first time in a fully reproducible way, controlled evaluation of avatar fingerprinting systems across multiple state-of-the-art synthesis pipelines and source datasets. This makes it possible to study whether current avatar fingerprinting systems truly capture identity-related behavioral cues or instead rely on generatoror dataset-specific artifacts.

The proposed benchmark and results achieved using two state-of-theart public avatar fingerprinting systems highlight two main findings. First, avatar fingerprinting is feasible under controlled conditions, supporting the hypothesis that identity-related motion cues can persist after avatar synthesis. Second, current avatar fingerprinting systems remain sensitive to both generator and dataset shift. These results indicate that present methods do not yet learn fully robust and invariant behavioral representations.

Overall, AVAPrintDB provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for studying avatar fingerprinting under diverse synthesis and data conditions. We hope it facilitates the development of more robust and practically useful avatar fingerprinting systems for authentication in avatar-mediated communication.

text:
RUI YANG, RUSHI LAN, ZHENRONG DENG, and XIAONAN LUO, The Guangxi Key

Laboratory of Image and Graphic Intelligent Processing, Guilin University of Electronic Technology,

Guilin, China

XIYAN SUN, The Nanning Research Institute, Guilin University of Electronic Technology,

Nanning, China

With the development of Metaverse technology, the avatar in Metaverse has faced serious security and privacy concerns. Analyzing facial features to distinguish between genuine and manipulated facial videos holds significant research importance for ensuring the authenticity of characters in the virtual world and for mitigating discrimination as well as preventing malicious use of facial data. To address this issue, the Facial Feature Points and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) deepfake video detection model is designed based on the clues of different FFPs distribution in real and fake videos and different displacement distances of real and fake FFPs between frames. The face video input is first detected by the BlazeFace model, and the face detection results are fed into the FaceMesh model to extract 468 FFPs. Then, the Lucas-Kanade (LK) optical flow method is used to track the points of the face, the face calibration algorithm is introduced to re-calibrate the FFPs, and the jitter displacement is calculated by tracking the FFPs between frames. Finally, the Ch is designed in the transformer, and the FFPs and FFP displacement are jointly classified through the ChT model. In this way, the designed ChT classifier is able to accurately and effectively identify deepfake videos. Experiments on open datasets clearly demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization capabilities of our approach.

text: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has resulted in the widespread integration of Metaverse technology into various aspects of entertainment, daily life, and education. Within this Metaverse environment, avatars confront substantial security and privacy challenges. Due to the close correlation between facial features and identity information, it is crucial to establish effective privacy protection measures through the analysis of facial features. By detecting forged faces in the virtual world, it is possible to identify manipulated faces with malicious and discriminatory intent, aiming to prevent gender, race, ethnic, and other imbalances. Simultaneously, Deepfake (DF) detection can be utilized to authenticate avatars, preventing identity theft or the deceptive misuse of avatars. If an avatar is identified as fake or manipulated, appropriate actions can be taken to mitigate potential risks.

section_path: Deepfake Video Detection Using Facial Feature Points and Ch-Transformer
text: Currently, DF videos, generated through adversarial networks, demonstrate an unprecedented level of authenticity. In the Metaverse, these DF creations typically fall into three primary categories: audio, video, and image manipulations, with video manipulations being the most widely recognized. This technique involves recording an individual and seamlessly replacing their facial features with those of another person using pre-existing video footage. This intricate process heavily relies on deep learning algorithms, which effectively blend facial images and videos to produce counterfeit content that is often imperceptible to the naked eye. It's worth noting that current DF technology primarily relies on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and its optimization models for its operation, representing a critical aspect of its functionality. ProGAN [10] and StyleGAN [16] are the two primary methods used to generate new synthetic faces. Fake videos are mainly divided into face replacement and expression exchange. Representative face replacement models include DeepFaceLab [34], FaceSwap (FS) [20], Face Swapping GAN [32], and DFs [19]. These models generate new synthetic videos by blending the image of a target person with existing video footage. DF, also known as facial reproduction, is currently popular with techniques, such as Face2Face (F2F) [44] and NeuralTextures (NTs) [43], where a facial expression from another person's face is replaced with the target's facial expression, such as changing the expression and movement to complete a fake "speech." The extensive application of DF technology, as evident from this, may pose significant security and privacy risks to virtual characters within the Metaverse.

section_path: Deepfake Video Detection Using Facial Feature Points and Ch-Transformer
text:
Given the aforementioned background, DF videos can be utilized to steal the identities of virtual characters in the Metaverse. They can impersonate individuals for fraudulent activities, damage others' reputations, and initiate malicious cybersecurity attacks. This may ultimately lead to a crisis of trust in virtual world technology. Many experts and scholars have conducted research in this field. Currently, there are two main methods for detecting DF videos. The first method is based on analyzing single frames of the video to determine whether it is real or fake by examining details, such as hair, pupil, and facial features. The work presented in this article is inspired by Sun et al. [41], who demonstrated that the jitter of facial key points between real and fake video frames differs, as illustrated in Figure 1. Thus, a combination of Facial Feature Points (FFPs) distribution and displacement jitter is utilized to predict whether a video is real or fake.

We design a DF detection model FFPs and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) for the Metaverse, which focuses on identifying inconsistencies between the distribution of FFPs on a face and the jitter displacements in real and fake videos. Our model classifies videos based on the distribution of FFPs and the jitter displacements between those points in each video frame, thereby determining whether the face in the video is real or fake. FFP-ChT consists of three parts, first, a FFPs extraction model is used to extract 468 individual FFPs in each frame of the video. Secondly, the movement displacement of FFPs is calculated using the LK optical flow tracking method. Finally, the ChT is used to jointly predict FFPs and their jitter displacement in each video frame. Experimental results show that our DF detection model is robust and achieves higher Accuracy (ACC) not only on simple videos but also on higher resolution video datasets. The main contributions of our work are as follows:

text: Similar to other AI tasks, the initial detection of fake face videos using single frame images has evolved from traditional methods to deep learning methods. Traditional methods include support vector machines [30], co-occurrence matrices [29], residual domain differences [21], and spectral differences [33] and have progressed to optical response heterogeneity and analysis of spatial domain features in images [37].

section_title: 2.1 Detection of DF Videos Based on Single-Frame Images
text: In the deep learning-based models, Jeon et al. introduced the Transferable GAN-images Detection framework, which applied transfer learning to GAN for the first time in generating image detection [14]. Further, Jeon proposed the fine-tuning neural network architecture, Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network, that incorporated a self-attention module to focus on the module and the undersampling layer. This method significantly enhanced the ACC [15]. Chen et al. found that both the luminance and chrominance components play important roles in detecting GAN-generated facial images. Therefore, considering both the luminance and chrominance components in the dual-color spaces can enhance the robustness of the model [5]. Hsu et al. utilized pair learning to detect deep forged images and transformed DenseNet into a two-flow network structure, which inputted paired information to train the common pseudo-feature network. The paired information then connected to the classification layer to detect the authenticity of the input image. It was noted that images generated by different GAN may have unknown image distortion, such as blur, noise, and JPEG compression [13]. Liu et al. found that large texture information is more robust to image distortion and proposed the GramNet model, which focuses on texture information as an essential clue for deep forgery image detection [27]. When new DF generation methods become available, many DF detection models' performance deteriorates. Thus, Khalid et al. proposed One-Class FakeDetect, which uses variational autoencoder to encode inputs as distributions in potential spaces [18]. Hinton et al. proposed a robust architecture composed of multiple capsules to solve the limitations of neural networks on inverse image problems. Capsule networks were applied to deep forgery detection [36]. Dual Spatial Pyramid for Exposing Face Warp Artifacts (DSP-FWA) model of Li et al. was limited by computational resources and production time, as the DF algorithm could only synthesize face images of fixed size and had to be affine distorted to match the face configuration of the source.

text: Liu et al. proposed a new block shuffling framework that consists of intra-block and inter-block transfer learning modules. The former improves the robustness of the network by intra-block transformation and overfits the problem by adversarial learning, while the latter encourages the network to learn local features through interblock shuffling and to model the semantic relevance of local features through refactoring [26]. The model high-frequency proposed by Luo et al. in 2021 improved the detection ACC by designing a multi-scale high-frequency feature extraction module, residual-guided spatial attention module, and cross-modal attention module [28]. Liu et al. proposed the Spatial-Phase Shallow Learning (SPSL) model, which captures upsampled artifacts of face forgery, improving the portability of face forgery detection [25]. Chen et al. proposed a Multi-Scale Patch Similarity Module (MPSM) to measure the similarity between local regional features and form a robust generalized similarity model [7]. They also proposed enhancing the "diversity" of forgery by synthesizing enhanced forgery with a pool of forgery configurations and enhancing the "sensitivity" to forgery by forcing models to predict forgery configurations [6]. Li et al. proposed the face X-ray model, which can classify true and false face videos by capturing the mixed boundary of forged images and the non-mixed boundary of real images. DF detection has typically been described as a classification problem based on cross-entropy loss, which emphasizes class-level differences rather than essential differences between real and fake faces, limiting the model's generalization in the invisible domain [22]. Sun et al. proposed a new face forgery detection framework called Dual Contrast Learning (DCL), which addresses the problem of local content inconsistency by constructing local region pairs in the instance. The issue of local content inconsistency is addressed by constructing local region pairs within the instance [39]. Gu et al. proposed the Hierarchical Contrastive Inconsistency Learning model, which can distinguish real faces from fake faces by deeply contrasting images [12].

text: Compared to DF detection based on image detail features, there have been fewer studies on DF detection based on video timing features, and the research in this area is relatively new. In light of the spatio-temporal inconsistency present in generated forged videos, Zhang et al. proposed a time-domain separation three-dimensional convolutional neural network, Temporal Dropout 3DCNN, which utilizes the inconsistent cues between video frames. This method exhibits excellent generalization ability and ACC compared to popular benchmarks [46]. Zheng et al. proposed an end-to-end framework comprising a full-time convolutional network. They focused on making the network learning time-agnostic and proposed to limit the ability of the network to handle spatial correlation. By limiting the spatial dimension, the network's evolution concentrates on time dependence. This method achieves better results in dataset training without any pre-training or manual operation [48]. In 2022, Zhang et al. proposed a simple yet effective patch-level method, spatio-temporal dropout Transformer, to fully utilize the spatio-temporal inconsistencies present in local facial areas of different frames in DF videos. The input video is extracted into a facial frame sequence, which is then reassembled into a patch pack and introduced into the visual converter to learn the differential representation of dynamic spatio-temporal cues in local facial areas describing different frames [47]. In 2021, Sun et al. proposed a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) classification algorithm model, LRNet, based on 68 human face landmarks, and introduced a new plug-and-play landmark calibration module to improve the ACC of facial geometric features and the effectiveness of time modeling [41]. Gu et al. studied the local motion of the image extensively and proposed a new sampling unit, Intra-Snippet Inconsistency Module, which uses bidirectional time difference operation and a learnable convolution kernel to mine short-term motion within each fragment. Their Snippet Inconsistency Module model achieved robust results in detecting DF videos [11].

Our proposed DF video detection model FFP-ChT consists of four components as shown in Figure 2. Firstly, the input video is divided into frames, and a set of frames of the video image is fed into the BlazeFace model for face detection. Then, the face detection results are fed into the FaceMesh model to extract 468 FFPs. The extracted FFPs are repositioned by the feature point Re-Calibration algorithm. Finally, the FFPs and the displacement sequences of frame are fed into the ChT designed in this article for classification and prediction. The prediction results of FFPs and the prediction results of FFPs displacement sequences are combined to predict whether the input video is real or fake.

Fig. 2. General diagram of the FFP-ChT model. The input video frames are processed as a group and passed through BlazeFace for face detection and then through FaceMesh for the extraction of 468 FFPs. The extracted feature points are further calibrated by the FFP Re-Calibration algorithm, which computes a sequence of feature point displacements between frames. The FFP and FFP displacement sequences are separately fed into the ChT for training and the resulting predictions are combined for the final output. Conv, Convolutional layer; Conv2d, Two-Dimensional (2D) Convolutional layer; PReLU, Parametric Rectified Linear Unit.

To obtain FFPs with high ACC and relatively small computational cost, the face detection model adopts BlazeFace, a lightweight face detection model proposed by Bazarevsky et al. in 2019 [2]. The BlazeFace structure is shown in Figure 2, which mainly consists of one convolutional layer, five Single BlazeBlocks, and six Double BlazeBlocks. The Single BlazeBlock and Double BlazeBlock structures are shown in Figure 3.

Single BlazeBlock initially splits the input feature map into two branches for processing. The first branch undergoes a Depthwise (DW) convolutional layer with a 5 � 5 convolution kernel, followed by a convolutional layer with a 1 � 1 convolution kernel. The second branch is optional and involves parameter reduction by max pooling. The outputs of the last two branches are then added using an activation function. Double BlazeBlock builds upon the Single BlazeBlock structure by adding a 5 � 5 DW convolutional layer and a 1 � 1 convolutional layer on top of it. The face feature map detected by BlazeFace is fed into the FaceMesh key point extraction model, which was proposed by Google in the MediaPipe library in 2020 [17]. The structure diagram of FaceMesh is depicted in Figure 4.

Fig. 4. FaceMesh model. It is mainly extracted by backbone, coord\_head outputs the prediction result, conf\_head outputs the confidence of the result, and finally adds the joint prediction.

The backbone of the FaceMesh key point extraction model consists primarily of a TwoDimensional (2D) convolutional layer (Conv2d) and Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU) activation functions, and a FaceMesh Block structure. The training results are predicted through two heads, with the coord\_head directly outputting the prediction results and with the conf\_head outputting the confidence level. Finally, the two results are combined to produce the final FFPs prediction result. The FaceMesh Block shown on the right of Figure 4. The feature images are passed into the FaceMesh Block structure. If the step size is 2, the MaxPooling layer is adopted; if the step size is not 2, the feature images are expanded by padding, inputted into two 2D convolutional Conv2d layers, and finally outputted by the PReLU activation function.

The BlazeFace model is used to detect the entire face in each frame of the input video and to compute the face position in the image. The face landmark model is then employed to extract FFPs with a detection confidence threshold of 0.5. Each FFP is defined by its position coordinates "G� ~", and the facial contour is outlined by these FFPs, with the landmark points aligned to their corresponding preset positions via affine transformation, as illustrated in Figure 5. The 468 extracted FFPs are primarily located in the eyes, nose, mouth, and face regions. The nasal region features the highest density of FFPs in the 2D feature point distribution after the affine transformation. The model analysis depicted in Figure 5 confirms that the selected FFPs conform to a normal distribution.

text: The Faceforensics,, (FF,,) dataset [35] consists of 1,000 raw videos downloaded from the internet, along with four corresponding versions of fake faces. The dataset comprises of videos with male and female subjects, with a ratio of 1 : 3 and 2 : 3, respectively. The resolution distribution is as follows: approximately 1/2 of the videos are in 480p, 3�8 in 720p, and 1�8 in 1080p. All videos contain a traceable, unobstructed front face that is used for automatic tampering to generate a real fake face. The videos were processed using one of four automatic face tamper methods, namely DFs, F2F, FS, NTs, and FaceShifter. As the primary aim is to assess the DF detection performance of the designed model, the DF subset is utilized for experimentation in this study.

text: Celeb-DF [24] is a recently proposed dataset with high-visual quality. The Celeb-DF dataset comprises of two versions: Celeb-DF(v1) and Celeb-DF(v2). In this experiment, Celeb-DF(v2) version was used. Celeb-DF(v1) contains 158 real videos and 795 fake videos, while Celeb-DF(v2) is a significant expansion over the v1 version, with 5,639 fake videos and 590 real videos based on publicly available YouTube clips from 59 celebrities of various genders, ages, and races. The average length of all videos is about 13 seconds, with a standard frame rate of 30 frames per second; 56.8% of the videos feature male subjects and 43.2% feature female subjects. The age distribution is as follows: 8.5% of the subjects are aged 60 or older, 30.5% are aged 50-60, 26.6% are in their 40s, 28.0% are in their 30s, and 6.4% are under 30. The racial distribution is as follows: 5.1% of the subjects are Asian, 6.8% are African American, and 88.1% are Caucasian. Additionally, the dataset features a wide range of variations in face size (in pixels), orientation, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. The fake face videos were generated by swapping each pair of faces of 59 subjects using an improved DF algorithm. As a result, the overall visual quality of the Celeb-DF dataset is significantly improved compared to the existing datasets.

4.2.1 Experimental Environment. The experiments presented in this article are conducted on the Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS operating system, utilizing a GeForce RTX 2080 Ti graphics processing unit with a graphics memory capacity of 12 GB. The CUDA version 9.2 and PyTorch 1.7.1 framework are utilized. The FF,, dataset is divided into a training set and a validation set using an 8:2 ratio, similar to the basic model. For the CelebDF dataset, the division method provided by the original authors is adopted. Additionally, the parameters used for all datasets are the same. The specific experimental parameters are set as follows: batch size of 1.024, learning rate of 0.001, 400 epochs for training the detection network based on the absolute location of key points, and 300 epochs for training the detection network based on the relative location of FFPs. During training, each video is divided into fixed 60 frame segments as a training sample. The key point information of each frame is mapped to a 128 dimensional vector, and position coding is carried out for each 60 frame training sample with a droprate of 0.1 for the position coding layer. Then, a Learnable embedding vectors (cls\_token) is added, and the data are passed through a Transformer encoder with a dropout layer of droprate = 0.1 for encoding. The specific parameters for the Transformer encoder are set as follows: the encoder had 1 layer, 8 attention heads, 512 dimensions for each attention head, 128 for the last layer normalization, and 2 for the output of the linear transformation layer.

4.2.2 Evaluation Metrics. To assess the efficacy of the model in discerning authentic and counterfeit facial videos, the evaluation metrics ACC and Area Under the Curve (AUC) are used. ACC represents the proportion of correctly predicted samples out of the total samples, while AUC represents the probability that a positive sample score is greater than a negative sample score. In the Celeb-DF(v2) dataset, there are 5639 fake videos and only 590 real videos, making the ACC evaluation index less reliable. text: In this article, to improve face privacy protection in the virtual world, we presented a new method for detecting DF videos that focuses on the inconsistency between the distribution of FFPs and their jitter displacements in real and fake videos. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DF detection model has good robustness, as it achieves higher ACC in video datasets with higher resolution and obtains better detection results in simple videos. With the evolution of the Metaverse, in the future, DF detection can assist in establishing a series of identity verification standards in the virtual world to ensure the authenticity of users' identities. Simultaneously, it is possible to explore DF detection that combines various sensors and data sources to enhance the validation of real identities, thereby improving the capability to detect forged faces and reducing deception in virtual spaces.

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: We propose a new comprehensive benchmark to revolutionize the current deepfake detection field to the next generation. Predominantly, existing works identify top-notch detection algorithms and models by adhering to the common practice: training detectors on one specific dataset (e.g., FF++ [62]) and testing them on other prevalent deepfake datasets. This protocol is often regarded as a "golden compass" for navigating SoTA detectors. But can these stand-out "winners" be truly applied to tackle the myriad of realistic and diverse deepfakes lurking in the real world? If not, what underlying factors contribute to this gap? In this work, we found the dataset (both train and test) can be the "primary culprit" due to the following: (1) forgery diversity: Deepfake techniques are commonly referred to as both face forgery (face-swapping and face-reenactment) and entire face synthesis (especially face). Most existing datasets only contain partial types of them, with limited forgery methods implemented (e.g., 2 swapping and 2 reenactment methods in FF++); (2) forgery realism: The dominated training dataset, FF++, contains out-of-date forgery techniques from the past four years. "Honing skills" on these forgeries makes it difficult to guarantee effective detection generalization toward nowadays' SoTA deepfakes; (3) evaluation protocol: Most detection works perform evaluations on one type, e.g., training and testing on face-swapping types only, which hinders the development of universal deepfake detectors.

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: To address this dilemma, we construct a highly diverse and large-scale deepfake detection dataset called DF40, which comprises 40 distinct deepfake techniques (10 times larger than FF++). We then conduct comprehensive evaluations using 4 standard evaluation protocols and 8 representative detection methods, resulting in over 2,000 evaluations. Through these evaluations, we provide an extensive analysis from various perspectives, leading to 7 new insightful findings contributing to the field. We also open up 4 valuable yet previously underexplored research questions to inspire future works. We release our dataset, code, and checkpoints at https://github.com/YZY-stack/DF40.

text:
Amidst this AIGC revolution, the ease of generating deepfakes 1 has become a "double-edged sword." Unfortunately, deepfake is often misused for manipulating one person's identity (face-swapping) or controlling facial expressions and movements in a portrait (face-reenactment). It can be particularly harmful as it may lead to severe digital crimes and undermine social trust. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a reliable system for detecting deepfakes.

Unfortunately, most existing detection methods can only handle a subset of deepfake types [65; 87]. To illustrate, in face-swapping deepfake detection, blending-based detectors [65; 43] have achieved SoTA results on existing face-swapping datasets (e.g., CDF [42]). But all these methods heavily rely on the assumption that existing face-swapping should share a blending step 2 . However, recent advancements in face-swapping (e.g., Simswap [9], FaceDancer [61]) directly generate all content (including the background) without blending. So "looking for" the specific blending artifacts for detecting the "non-blending" forgeries such as Simswap could be unrealistic. Regrettably, this crucial observation may not be well-known in the field, as most existing face-swapping deepfake datasets [62; 17; 42] involve blending in their fake data. Similarly, many existing face-reenactment generators (e.g., LIA [82]) and all entire-image-synthesis generators (e.g., DDPM [24]) are also without any blending. Hence, developing detectors on these blend-only datasets might limit the model's potential ability to detect a broad range of deepfake types. In a real-world scenario with unpredictability and complexity, creating such a "unified" detector is essential. However, this issue has persistently been challenging, as most existing datasets either contain limited types or are specific to forgery types (see Tab. 1).

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text:
Therefore, we realize that a diverse and comprehensive dataset is the true key to "unlock" the potential of ideal deepfake detection. To this end, we "jump" from the previous protocol settings (e.g., train and test solely on face-swapping fakes) and propose a new comprehensive dataset called DF40. Our main contribution can be generally summarized as two folds: (1) Our DF40 implements 40 different deepfake techniques, including face-swapping, face-reenactment, entire face synthesis, and face editing. We even include the just-released DiT [54], PixArt-α [8], and highly popular software DeepFaceLab [14] and HeyGen [23] to simulate real-world deepfakes; (2) We introduce 4 standard protocols for evaluations and show 8 insightful findings to the field. We also open up new research questions and topics to inspire future research toward next-generation deepfake detection.

1 Deepfake is a term derived from "deep" (the use of deep nets) and "fake" (does not exist). Our scope mainly focuses on face deepfakes but shows the promising in detecting other non-face deepfakes such as arts.

2 Blending the altered (deepfake-generated) face into an existing background image.

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: Based on previous survey [50], deepfake techniques can be typically classified into four types: face-swapping (FS), face-reenactment (FR), entire face synthesis (EFS), and face editing (FE). (1) Face-swapping: This paper classifies the face-swapping technique into two domains: DF-family and FS-family. (i) DF-family involves creating a mask around the facial region (some even include the neck [46]) and blending the generated deepfake face back into the background image using that mask. Most existing and famous face forgery datasets, such as FF-DF [62], CDF [42] and DFDC [16], belong to this line. (ii) FS-family methods represent another significant category in face-swapping deepfake generation. These methods typically involve the use of an identity-background encoder. It disentangles a face image's identity and background information during encoding. Notably, these methods directly generate all content, even the background. Many recent face-swapping research works [85; 9] are within this line. (2) Face-reenactment: Generally, this technique can be used to modify source faces, imitating the actions or expressions of another face. Differing from face-swapping, face-reenactment techniques are rarely considered in existing datasets. Two commonly used reenactment-based forgeries are Face2Face [72] and NeuralTextures [71]. These two forgeries are implemented in the FF++ dataset. Due to the amazingly rapid development of the AIGC technologies (e.g., Digital Human), these relatively old-fashioned methods cannot represent the modern' SoTA reenactment methods. Our DF40 implements 13 face-reenactment methods in total, including the classical animation [67; 68], SoTA's audio-based driven methods [92; 55], imagebased driven methods [82; 26; 5].

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: We also include the well-known best face generation technique, HeyGen [23], in our dataset for evaluation. (3) Entire Face Synthesis: This technique can be generally treated as "Face AIGC." With the rapid development of AIGCs, this technique has achieved remarkably notable improvement. The two widely used technologies to generate synthesis faces are GAN (e.g., VQGAN [20]) and Diffusion models (e.g., StableDiffusion [59]). (4) Face Editing: This technique aims to modify the facial attributes (e.g., age and gender) of the given face images. Most of these works utilize the latent code of StyleGAN [35] to perform editing during GAN inversion.

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: Most earlier public deepfake datasets published before 2021 [37; 91; 17; 42; 62; 13] generate deepfakes using only the face-swapping technique that involves a blending process. Also, these datasets contain only single or no more than 4 specific manipulation approaches. Notably, DFDC [16] implements 7 deepfake approaches and extends the data scale to the million-level. After that, ForgeryNet [22] applies 15 methods to create forgery data with a million-level data scale. However, with the advent of AIGCs such as diffusion-based generators, producing realistic content has become increasingly popular and widely seen on social media. Consequently, whether a detector trained on older forgery methods can generalize to today's SoTA deepfakes is uncertain. In response, many recent works [32; 69] have begun to focus on current generative models. document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: Research Scope and Summary of DF40. In this work, our scope specifically focuses on face deepfake detection, including face-swapping (FS), face-reenactment (FR), entire face synthesis (EFS), and face editing (FE). Natural image synthesis (such as art) is not within our scope, but we show the potential of using model training on face deepfake to detect these AIGC-generated images. DF40 dataset provides 40 deepfake approaches with 4 different types: FS, FR, EFS, and FE. For FS and FR, we provide video format data (over 0.1M video clips in total), and image format for EFS and FE (over 1M+ images in total). We also introduce several latest/popular generation techniques (e.g., PixArt-α [8] in 2024) and online software (e.g., HeyGen [23], DeepFaceLab [14; 29]). Furthermore, some classical and representative methods are also included, e.g., FOMM [67]. Our dataset shows the advantages in both data diversity and scale (see Tab. 1).

text: Original Data Collection and Deepfake Data Generation. (1) Real Data: We consider two mainstream and popular deepfake datasets: FF++ [62] (c23 version) and CDF [42] as our original data. The rationale behind this selection is that most previous research [40; 65; 90] follows the evaluation protocol of training on FF++ and testing on CDF. By utilizing these datasets for training and evaluation, we can adhere to previous works and verify if their conclusions and methods still hold in the context of our new dataset. We also provide real data from other existing datasets (e.g., CelebA [47]) to facilitate the unknown domain evaluations (see Tab. 2 for details). We show more details of these original face datasets in the Appendix. (2) Fake Data: To guarantee the diversity of deepfake approaches in the proposed DF40, we introduce and implement 40 distinct deepfake techniques, which are listed in Tab. 2. text: All pre-processing and training codebases in this work adhere to DeepfakeBench [90] to align the standardized settings. The details of dataset configuration, algorithm implementation, and full training can be seen in the Appendix. For detection selection, we choose the classical baseline Xception [12] with four SoTA detectors (SRM [48], SPSL [44], RECCE [6], RFM [75]) that use Xception as the backbone. In this manner, we aim to revisit the extra improvement over the baseline under our setting. We also consider the blending-based detector that uses the blending image (BI) for training, which creates pseudo-fakes by image blending, without using the actual deepfake data. We use SBI [65] to implement the blending-based detector. Note that the original SBI paper only uses BI for training, so we do not re-train it using our DF40 in evaluations.

text:
In this work, we conduct evaluations under four standard protocols: Cross-forgery evaluation (Protocol-1), Cross-domain evaluation (Protocol-2), Toward unknown forgery or domain evaluation (Protocol-3), and One-Verse-All (OvA) evaluation (Protocol-4). From these evaluations, we list 8 critical findings via empirical observations or in-depth analysis, as follows.

Finding-1: Asymmetric performance drop among different forgery types (fake regions matter). From Tab. 3, we observe that the performance drop between FS and FR is moderate but more significant between these two and EFS. Specifically, model training on FS yields higher results (around 0.8) on EFS, while training on EFS only achieves about 0.6 on FS. To understand the underlying reason for this finding, we provide the following detailed explanations: One possible explanation is that FS can exhibit both localized and global forgeries, while EFS is restricted to global forgeries, making EFS less diverse in scope compared to FS. As a result, training a model on EFS might not be sufficient to capture the localized fake artifacts present in FS. For example, some localized FS (such as DeepFakes of FF++ [62]) only contain fake artifacts within the facial region, but a model trained on EFS might be biased to "expect" artifacts across the entire image, including the background, resulting in a lower result on FS. To verify our claim, we consider using t-SNE for visualizing the latent distribution of 'real', 'whole-fake', and 'face-fake'. The t-SNE (Fig. 4) results show that a well-trained EFS detection model can easily distinguish the whole-fake from real images. However, the localized version, including face-fake and mouth-fake, appears much more similar to real images, making it more challenging to detect compared to the whole-fake. This experiment qualitatively verifies the significance of the fake region in detection.

Finding-2: Existing well-designed (SoTA) detectors may not have obvious advantages over the baseline. In our experiments, SRM, SPSL, RECCE, and RFM, all state-of-the-art deepfake detectors using Xception as their backbone, achieve results similar to the simple baseline Xception. This implies that these SoTA models might only learn sub-optimal forgery features and lack clear advantages over the baseline, although these SoTAs show higher results on previous datasets, e.g., DFDC. In other words, although these well-designed SoTA detectors achieve higher scores than the Xception (baseline) when testing on CDF [42], they cannot maintain a consistent advantage over the baseline when testing on other forgeries. This highlights the remaining generalization issue.

document_title: DF40: Toward Next-Generation Deepfake Detection
text: Finding-3: CLIP excels in deepfake detection than other baselines (such as Xception). Outperforming other SoTA detectors and the Xception baseline across all scenarios, CLIP (both base and large versions) demonstrates the power of pre-training in deepfake detection. This highlights the benefits of pre-training before fine-tuning on the deepfake detection task. However, why can CLIP outperform the Xception by a notable margin? We analyze this point in the following content from the view of real face distribution. We analyze the learned features of the three models (CLIP-base, CLIP-large, Xception), as visualized in Fig. 7. (1) We see that both versions of CLIP learn more informative features that can gather some real samples into several different "groups" (see HeyGen and MidJourney), while the real features of Xception mix all of them together. Leveraging large-scale pre-training, CLIP can capture more informative facial features (e.g., ID) about real faces and thus "know" that these features are unrelated to deepfakes, while Xception could be overfitted to ID, as evidenced by [19]. (2) Between the large and base versions, CLIP-large's real samples are closer to each other (see WhichisReal), suggesting it learns more comprehensive features of real faces. We also see that CLIP-large can implicitly "separate and align" different forgeries and data domains ("orthogonal" in WhichisReal), with no need for explicit constraints as [70].

text:
Finding-4: Forgery methods and data domains together contribute to discriminative forgery artifacts. A significant performance drop is observed when both forgeries and domains change. For example, Xception training on FS (FF) achieves only 0.657 and 0.642 on FR (CDF) and EFS (CDF), respectively. These results are significantly lower (nearly a 20% drop) compared to results on FS (CDF) and FR (FF), which involve crossing only one of the domains or forgeries. This suggests that both factors together contribute to discriminative forgery artifacts for distinguishing real and fake.

To intuitively convey our conclusions, we draw a causal graph to illustrate the causal relationship of how domain (D) and forgery method (F) influence the model's generalization (R). The causal graph is presented in Fig. 5. Mathematically, the model's generalization result R can be expressed as a function of these intermediate variables: R = f(X1, X2, X3), where X1 = g(D) represents the domain-specific influence, X3 = h(F) represents the forgery method-specific influence, and X2 = k(D, F) represents the combined influence of both domain and forgery method. Each of these variables X1, X2, and X3 captures different aspects of how D and F interact to impact the overall performance R. The functions g, h, and k are mappings that quantify the respective influences: X1 = g(D), X3 = h(F), and X2 = k(D, F). Finally, the result R is determined by integrating these influences:

Finding-6: SBI could be viewed as an "anomaly detection" model. SBI [65] (a blending-based detection) could be considered an "anomaly detection" model, which might utilize the real features for classifying fakes. Results in Fig. 6(a) show that when forgery samples appear significantly different from real samples, SBI classifies them as anomalies (forgery samples), likely because the pseudo-fake samples generated by SBI closely resemble their original real counterparts. In other words, SBI creates more realistic fake samples that are more similar to the real, encouraging the detection model to learn a more robust real representation than the baseline.

Finding-7: CLIP-large shows the potential to generalize to some non-face deepfakes when trained only on face data. In additional to evaluate on the face deepfakes, we also evaluate non-face-domain deepfakes (natural image synthesis) using the widely-used GenImag edataset to determine if models trained on face-domain data can transfer to non-face-domain detection. In Tab. 19, surprisingly, CLIP-large achieves a 0.746 AUC on previously unseen non-face deepfakes, while Xception only reaches a 0.535 AUC, near chance levels. This highlights that CLIP-large might learn some transferable (EFS) forgery features that are not related to the face content.

Why AMore Diverse Deepfake Dataset Is Crucial for Current Deepfake Detector? In our work, we propose the DF40 dataset, with highly diverse deepfake approaches. Here, we aim to qualitatively verify why such a highly diverse dataset is extremely crucial for current deepfake detectors. The results in Fig. 8 show that CFDA [43] (latest SoTA) achieves significant advantages over other methods on existing datasets, but it performs comparably or even worse than other detectors. This emphasizes the necessity of constructing a dataset that encompasses a greater variety of deepfake methods and types. Without such a highly diverse dataset for evaluation, we would only be seeing "the tip of the iceberg." In other words, the current SoTA may not be the definitive "winner."

Are Super-Resolution Images Fake? Here, we explore whether a super-resolution (SR) image will be considered fake or real by the detection model. This question is important for two reasons: (1) many deepfake software programs involve an SR operation to enhance the resolution of generated faces (e.g., FaceFusion 3 ), and (2) Most existing SR methods [81] are based on deep generative models such as GAN. Therefore, the output of SR methods can also contain generative artifacts that might be similar to those in deepfake images. We use GFPGAN to perform SR on the self-reconstruction images (SRI), where we use SimSwap [9] to perform face-swap to the same ID. Results in Tab. 8 show that SR has a significant impact on fake images, particularly for EFS and FE methods. As demonstrated in the table, models trained on FS and EFS exhibit more than a 20% point improvement for the SRI after applying super-resolution. This suggests that SR operations may introduce noticeable generative artifacts that can be detected by models trained on EFS and FE.

Exploration of Frequency Artifacts in Different Types of Deepfakes. Here, we explore whether there exist common fake patterns in the frequency domain. following [77], we compute the average frequency spectra of high-pass filtered images. Results in Fig. 9 show that although the deepfake types differ, they can show similar patterns/artifacts in the average spectra. For instance, methods from FS (i.e., SimSwap [9], BlendFace [66], InSwap) show similar "checkboard" patterns that can also be observed in EFS (i.e., SD1.5 [59], VQGAN [20]) and FE (i.e., e4e [73]). This observation highlights the need to further explore whether and why forgeries with different types can exhibit similar patterns in frequency.

AModel Bias Toward the Resolution Gap Between Real and Fake. In our previous experiments (see Tab. 5), we observe anti-intuitive phenomena: models training on FR achieve very low AUC (much lower than 0.5) on StyleCLIP. After investigating the underlying reason, we found that the unaligned resolution between the real and fake classes introduces a model bias, that is, higher resolution, higher probability to be real. Specifically, we observe that the training real data (FF++) obviously contains more high-frequency components (higher resolution) compared to the training fake data (FR). This noticeable resolution gap between real and fake data could be inevitably captured by the model [56], leading the model to potentially adopt a trivial solution: "Low resolution implies fake." In contrast, during testing, the fake data (StyleCLIP) contains significantly more high-frequency components (higher resolution) than the testing real data used for testing. We provide a frequency visualization as evidence to validate this claim (see our Appendix). This bias leads the model to make an inconsistent decision, resulting in the anomaly in AUC.
